summary: This document defines the IP-Only LAN Service (IPLS), a variant of Virtual Private LAN Service (VPLS) for cases where the interconnected systems are all IP hosts or routers rather than LAN switches. It is now historic.

plainLanguage.summary: Some office networks only carry internet traffic, not other kinds. This describes a simplified way to join such networks across a city. It is now historic and no longer used.

questions: what is ipls ip-only lan service
how does ipls differ from vpls
subtitle: A simplified Virtual Private LAN Service designed for connecting IP-only networks.

tldr.problem: Virtual Private LAN Service (VPLS) requires PE routers to perform complex MAC address learning and aging functions borrowed from Ethernet switches. For networks containing only IP hosts and routers (not LAN switches), these bridging functions are unnecessary complexity.
tldr.mechanism: IP-Only LAN Service (IPLS) simplifies VPLS by discovering MAC addresses through control-plane signaling instead of data-plane learning, and forwarding based on MAC lookup without requiring general bridging functionality. Unicast traffic uses one pseudowire per destination CE, while multicast and broadcast use a shared multicast pseudowire.
tldr.outcome: IPLS proved the concept, but newer hardware eventually made full VPLS simpler. The document is Historic, though its architectural ideas influenced later work like Ethernet VPN and data center networking applications.

facts.label: Forwarding basis
facts.value: MAC address lookup with pseudowire label

facts.label: Multicast PW per IPLS
facts.value: Exactly one per PE per instance

today: RFC 7436 is Historic. IPLS was designed to simplify VPLS for IP-only networks, but newer hardware eventually supported full VPLS more effectively. The concepts have been adopted in other technologies such as Ethernet VPN and data center networking, but this document is published as a historic record of the design.

sections.title: IPLS: IP-Only LAN Service
sections.content:
RFC 7436 specifies IP-Only LAN Service (IPLS), a simplified variant of Virtual Private LAN Service (VPLS) optimized for cases where the interconnected systems are IP hosts or IP routers only, not Ethernet LAN switches. VPLS normally requires PE (Provider Edge) routers to learn MAC addresses from data plane traffic using Ethernet bridge functions. IPLS avoids this complexity by discovering MAC addresses via control-plane signaling.

In an IPLS, Provider Edge routers still forward frames based on destination MAC address, but the MAC forwarding tables are populated via LDP (Label Distribution Protocol) signaling rather than through the IEEE bridge learning procedures. This allows PE routers designed primarily as IP routers to provide a multipoint LAN connectivity service without implementing full Ethernet switch functionality.

The original intent was to provide an alternative to VPLS for PE routers unable to perform MAC address learning in the data plane. However, newer hardware eventually supported full VPLS functionality more simply. The document notes that IPLS concepts are still valuable and have been adopted in newer work such as Ethernet VPN and data center applications. No further updates are planned, and this document is published as a historic record of the ideas.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of routers learning who is connected by watching messages, you tell each router who its local computers are. Then routers can forward messages using MAC addresses without acting like switches.

sections.title: Service Architecture and Topology
sections.content:
An IPLS instance interconnects geographically dispersed customer sites across a provider network, making them appear as a single LAN broadcast domain. At each site, Customer Edge (CE) devices (IP hosts or routers) connect to a Provider Edge (PE) router via an attachment circuit (AC), which may be a physical Ethernet port or a VLAN.

Each IPLS instance requires three key types of connectivity. Unicast pseudowires carry IP unicast traffic from remote PEs to one specific local CE. The PE creates one unicast pseudowire for each locally attached CE. These are unidirectional, forming a multipoint-to-point tree with remote PE devices as leaves and the local PE as root. Traffic flows from all remote sources toward the specific local CE destination.

A single multicast pseudowire per IPLS instance at each PE carries IP multicast and broadcast traffic, ARP frames, and IPv6 Neighbor Discovery frames. This creates a multipoint-to-point tree where remote PEs are leaves. The PE replicates multicast frames received from any AC or unicast pseudowire to all other ACs and to the multicast pseudowire.

Unlike VPLS where the egress PE looks up the destination MAC to determine the egress AC, in IPLS the egress AC is entirely determined by the ingress pseudowire label, simplifying the forwarding logic significantly.
sections.plainLanguage: Each office connects to a router. One virtual connection sends regular messages to one office. Another connection broadcasts announcements to all offices. Routers use label tags to know where messages go instead of learning who is where.

sections.title: CE Discovery and Pseudowire Signaling
sections.content:
When an attachment circuit becomes operational, the PE enters a CE discovery phase, examining received multicast and broadcast Ethernet frames. For IPv4, the PE snoops ARP frames to learn the MAC and IP address of each CE. For IPv6, the PE examines Neighbor Solicitation, Neighbor Advertisement, Router Solicitation, and Router Advertisement messages.

Once a CE is discovered, the PE advertises its MAC address and optionally its IP address to all remote PE peers participating in the same IPLS instance using LDP Label Mapping messages. For unicast pseudowires carrying IP traffic, the PE uses IP Layer 2 Transport encapsulation. For multicast pseudowires carrying Ethernet frames, the PE uses Ethernet encapsulation.

The PE must include a MAC Address TLV (Type-Length-Value) in the Label Mapping message when establishing unicast pseudowires; absence of this parameter causes label release. The PE may optionally include an IP Address TLV to signal the CE's IPv4 or IPv6 address. If a PE receives an Address Family type mismatch (e.g., expects IPv4 but receives IPv6), it must reject the pseudowire establishment with a specific status code.

The multicast pseudowire is the principal PW in each IPLS instance, representing the instance as a whole. The lifetime of all unicast pseudowires depends on the multicast PW; if the multicast PW ceases to exist, all associated unicast PWs are removed.
sections.plainLanguage: When a computer connects, the router watches for network announcements to learn its address. Then the router tells all other routers: send messages to this office for this computer. If a computer stops responding, the router forgets it.

sections.title: Forwarding and Frame Processing
sections.content:
IPLS forwarding handles different traffic types distinctly. For unicast IP traffic, the PE looks up the destination MAC address in its forwarding table. If a match is found, the packet is forwarded to the associated egress pseudowire. Packets received from a unicast pseudowire are forwarded to the egress AC with the MAC header prepended; the destination MAC is looked up in the table and the source MAC is set to the PE's own MAC address.

For multicast and broadcast IP traffic, frames received from an AC are replicated to all other ACs and the multicast pseudowire. Frames received from the multicast pseudowire are replicated to all egress ACs associated with that IPLS instance.

ARP packets are forwarded from ACs to multicast pseudowires in Ethernet frame format. Both ARP requests and responses are sent over the multicast pseudowire. When an ARP packet is received from an AC, a copy is submitted to the control plane for learning the CE's MAC address and optionally its IP address. All Ethernet packets received from the multicast pseudowire are forwarded to all ACs; these packets are not submitted to the control plane.

IPv6 Neighbor Discovery (ND) and (Inverse) Neighbor Discovery (IND) packets from an AC are replicated to other ACs and multicast pseudowires in native Ethernet format. A copy is also submitted to the control plane for CE learning. This allows IPv6 devices to discover each other and resolve IPv6 addresses to MAC addresses across the IPLS domain.
sections.plainLanguage: Regular messages go one way to one office based on the address table. Announcements and discovery messages go to all offices. When a computer introduces itself, the router remembers it. All messages keep their Ethernet addresses so offices stay connected.

sections.title: Configuration and Applicability
sections.content:
Each PE router is configured with one or more IPLS service instances, each associated with a unique VPN-ID. For each IPLS instance, a set of attachment circuits (ACs) is identified. Each AC can be associated with only one IPLS instance.

The PE can be optionally configured with a local MAC address to use as the source MAC when forwarding IP packets from a pseudowire to an AC. By default, the PE uses the MAC address of the customer-facing Ethernet interface itself.

IPLS simplifies VPLS by making several restrictions. The service is intended for IP traffic only and must not be used to interconnect CE devices that are themselves LAN switches. Instead, CEs must be IP hosts or IP routers. This restriction is acceptable in many environments given IP's dominance in modern networks.

An IPLS domain may use various tunneling technologies to carry pseudowires between PE routers, including MPLS, Generic Routing Encapsulation (GRE), or Layer 2 Tunneling Protocol version 3 (L2TPv3). PE routers in the same IPLS instance are interconnected via these tunneling mechanisms to form the virtual LAN service.
sections.plainLanguage: Each office network gets a unique number and a list of network ports. You set these up once on the routers. The system only works for IP messages and only when offices have computers and routers, not switches. The connection between routers can use different technologies.
